svg.title: Why a std Mutex guard must not be held across an await
svg.desc: Two timelines on one Tokio worker thread. Top, the pattern used in PhantomCache: task A locks a shard, does a short synchronous step, drops the guard, then awaits; task B runs and can take the lock. Bottom, the forbidden pattern: task A holds the guard across an await, task B on the same thread tries to lock and blocks the thread, so A cannot resume on that thread.
svg.text: One worker thread, time flows left to right
A. What the code does (allowed)
Task A: lock shard,
register, DROP guard
Task A: .await (waits
for oneshot), thread free
Task B: lock same
shard, works, drops
Task C: other work
(no lock needed)
Task A resumes: lock,
finalize, drop guard
Lock is held only for a short, synchronous, bounded section. Shaded = a std Mutex guard is alive.
B. What must not be written (hazard)
Task A: lock shard ... guard STILL ALIVE ... .await
(task is parked, but the guard is not released)
Task B (same thread): lock shard -> BLOCKS the
OS thread; A cannot be polled here to release it
Result on a one-thread runtime: deadlock. On a multi-thread runtime: stalls and lost throughput while A is parked.
Rust help: std::sync::MutexGuard is not Send, so a spawned task or an Axum handler that holds one across an .await
normally fails to compile. That is a compiler rule about Send, not a proof that no such code exists in the tree.
PhantomCache uses std::sync::Mutex (not tokio::sync::Mutex) for shards because every critical section is short and has
no I/O. Cost of that choice: a slow section (a long sweep scan, G4A-03) blocks a worker thread, not just one task.
